page: Amazon Web Services r7a.xlarge is a memory-optimized instance powered by an AMD EPYC 9R14 processor. It features 4 dedicated physical cores and 4 vCPUs running at 3.7 GHz, utilizing the x86_64 architecture. The instance is equipped with 32.0 GB of DDR5 memory operating at 5 GHz, providing a resource density of 8.0 GB of RAM per core. It operates on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, has a baseline network bandwidth of 2 Gbps, and does not include local storage or dedicated GPUs.

Benchmark results indicate strong single-core performance, with stress-ng single-core CPU testing and bzip3 single-threaded decompression scoring in the top 25%. Multi-core operations, such as stress-ng multi-core CPU performance and Geekbench multi-core compiling, fall within the average range. While cached small-block memory read bandwidth is average at 592.0 GB/sec, uncached large-block read bandwidth is weak at 37.49 GB/sec, representing a potential bottleneck for large out-of-cache data structures.

Given its high memory-to-vCPU ratio and strong single-threaded capabilities, the r7a.xlarge is suited for memory-intensive workloads, database operations, and text processing. However, its weak performance in medium-sized LLM inference (7B model) and uncached memory reads makes it less suitable for large-scale AI models or memory-bound streaming applications. Qualitatively, it offers a balanced cost-to-resource profile for enterprise applications requiring high DDR5 memory capacity without the overhead of high vCPU counts.
description: Amazon Web Services r7a.xlarge is a memory-optimized instance featuring 4 dedicated physical cores on an AMD EPYC 9R14 processor running at 3.7 GHz. It is equipped with 32.0 GB of high-speed 5 GHz DDR5 memory, yielding 8.0 GB of RAM per core, and runs on the Nitro hypervisor with a 2 Gbps baseline network speed. The instance lacks local storage and GPUs. Performance benchmarks show strong single-core CPU capabilities and text processing, while multi-core execution and database operations remain average. A key tradeoff is its weak uncached large-block memory read bandwidth of 37.49 GB/sec and low throughput for medium 7B LLM inference. This instance is well-suited for memory-intensive enterprise applications, database hosting, and text processing tasks that benefit from dedicated CPU allocation and high-speed DDR5 RAM without requiring massive parallel compute resources.
